idiom_name: async attempt loop with try await Task.sleep(nanoseconds:) and a capped jitter draw
implementation_notes: Swift has no retry or schedule API, so the realization is a hand-written loop that awaits Task.sleep(nanoseconds:), which Apple documents as suspending the current task for at least the duration, throwing CancellationError when the task is cancelled, and not blocking the underlying thread - precisely the primitive backoff needs in async code. The delay arithmetic (base * 2^(attempt-1), capped, jittered with Double.random) and the budget are yours, and the elapsed budget must be measured with a monotonic clock (ContinuousClock/SuspendingClock) rather than Date. In GCD-era code the same loop is built on DispatchQueue.asyncAfter with explicit cancellation, and third-party networking stacks add request-level retry hooks for HTTP specifically - neither replaces the schedule.
pitfalls: Task.sleep throws CancellationError when the task is cancelled; a catch clause that swallows it turns cooperative cancellation into a tight retry loop.
Structuring the retry as DispatchQueue.asyncAfter closures with captured state lets the closure outlive the caller's scope, so an abandoned request still fires its next attempt.
A Date-based budget can jump with wall-clock adjustments; measure the elapsed time with ContinuousClock or SuspendingClock.
